summary:
FarmBits is a global decision-support platform designed to bridge the "last mile" gap between complex satellite data and everyday agricultural management. To address the "Field Shift" challenge, we developed a three-layered prediction engine that integrates 30 years of daily NASA POWER climate data, SoilGrids, and FAO agronomic models to generate optimized 3-year crop rotation plans.

Our solution delivers these insights through two seamless interfaces: an interactive Web App for deep historical climate analytics, and a multimodal Telegram Bot that provides real-time field alerts and agronomic advice directly to the farmer's smartphone in their native language.

This project is vital because climate change has outpaced traditional crop rotation cycles, leaving farmers to plan future harvests in the dark. By translating raw NASA Earth observation data into clear, actionable, and localized guidance without requiring technical expertise, FarmBits democratizes climate adaptation. It empowers farmers worldwide to maximize resilience, protect soil health, and secure their livelihoods against unpredictable environmental shifts.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

  • FarmBits is a global decision-support platform that translates raw NASA Earth observation data into actionable, 3-year crop rotation plans for farmers.
  • The system operates on a deterministic, three-layered prediction engine written in Python.
  • Layer 1 relies on 30 years of daily NASA POWER climate data, SoilGrids, and FAO agronomic models to calculate water available in the soil, climate-derived planting windows, and hydro-climatic risks globally.
  • Layer 2 enriches the global analysis with FAOSTAT country-level yields, pricing, and global crop calendars.
  • Layer 3 utilizes national adapters, such as IBGE, CONAB, and ZARC for Brazil, to achieve municipal-level precision when available.
  • The platform features two synchronized interfaces: an interactive Web App built in Streamlit for deep analytics, and a Telegram bot that allows farmers to interact via voice notes, text, or photos in their native language.
  • An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server seamlessly connects the bot's Groq LLM to the core global engine, enabling the AI to execute mathematical tools and return accurate data to the farmer.

What benefits does it have?

  • The tool bypasses the steep learning curve of traditional GIS software, which currently keeps the adoption of crop simulation models under 1% among irrigating farmers in the US.
  • By delivering insights through a simple conversational interface, the system can compress the cost of rural technical extension from an average of $35.00 per farmer down to less than $1.00.
  • It provides side-by-side comparisons of different 3-year crop rotation plans based on specific metrics like water risk, soil health, and financial relative scores.
  • The system proactively tracks the water balance and alerts the farmer about potential drought stress before critical stages, such as flowering, occur.

What is the intended impact of the project?

  • The project aims to bridge the "last mile" digital divide, reaching smallholders and marginal farmers who lack computers, stable internet access, or technical literacy in developing nations.
  • It empowers farmers to maximize land use efficiency and regenerate soil organic matter through optimized, climate-resilient crop rotations.
  • Ultimately, it helps rural communities mitigate the financial risks of crop failures caused by climate change, sudden droughts, or heatwaves.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • The core global engine and the MCP server were developed entirely using the Python programming language.
  • We integrated the NASA POWER API to access daily climate data over a 30-year period and cached the responses to optimize performance.
  • Soil data was sourced from SoilGrids, and we utilized FAO-56 crop parameters alongside datasets like FAOSTAT, IBGE, ZARC, and CONAB.
  • The conversational bot was powered by the Groq API, utilizing models like openai/gpt-oss-120b or llama-3.3-70b-versatile via the Responses API for native Remote MCP tool execution.
  • We used meta-llama/llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct for vision analysis of crop photos and whisper-large-v3-turbo for transcribing the farmer's audio messages.
  • The user interfaces were built using Streamlit for the web application and python-telegram-bot for the mobile conversational experience.
  • Both interfaces share a common SQLite database (db.sqlite) to synchronize farm locations, active alerts, and field observation pins on the map.

How is your project creative?

  • FarmBits pioneers a "Zero-UI" Geospatial-RAG approach by moving complex satellite analytics out of static institutional dashboards and into multimodal messaging apps.
  • The engine is capable of dynamically calculating safe planting windows based purely on NASA climate data, specifically evaluating the start of the rainy season alongside the minimum and maximum temperature thresholds of the chosen crop.
  • This climate-derived fallback mechanism ensures the system works globally, even in regions where local governmental agricultural data is entirely nonexistent.
  • To prevent AI hallucinations, we established a strict architectural rule where the LLM only formats the text, while every number, risk percentage, and date is generated strictly by the deterministic NASA-powered Python core.

What factors did your team consider?

  • We considered the physical limitations of Earth observation satellites, such as how persistent cloud cover blinds optical sensors during the main rainy seasons in tropical agricultural frontiers.
  • We recognized that traditional agricultural platforms fail to reach the final user because they are designed from a top-down perspective for governments, insurers, or programmers, rather than offering direct prescriptive recommendations to farmers.
  • We addressed the issue of the rural digital divide by ensuring the tool could be accessed via mobile phones without requiring a broadband connection or any prior GIS expertise.
  • We factored in the etiological ambiguity of satellite signals, ensuring that field photos could be cross-referenced with the local water balance to help the farmer distinguish between abiotic water stress and biotic pest attacks.
